structured_output.hypothesis: If all living things share a common chemical and cellular basis, a substantial set of protein-coding gene families (orthologous groups) must be present in nearly all sampled species spanning the cellular domains of life, with core functions in translation, replication and metabolism.
structured_output.pass_criterion: In the COG2024 release, at least 50 COGs are present in at least 90% of the 2,103 bacterial and 193 archaeal genomes, and at least 80% of these universal COGs are annotated to core information-processing or metabolic functional categories (J, K, L, C, E, F, G, H, I, O).
structured_output.fail_criterion: Fewer than 10 COGs are present in at least 90% of genomes, or fewer than 50% of those near-universal COGs fall in core information-processing or metabolic functional categories.
structured_output.interpretation: Darwin's 'chemical composition', 'cellular structure' and 'laws of growth and reproduction' are mapped to conserved molecular machinery: genes of shared orthologous families (translation, replication, transcription, core metabolism) present across genomes. 'Germinal vesicles' (the nucleus of the egg cell) is reinterpreted as the universal presence of heritable genetic material and its replication machinery. The poison example is not tested here. Limitation: COG covers only bacteria and archaea, not eukaryotes, so it tests universality across prokaryotic domains and is a partial test of 'all living things'. Eukaryote coverage would need a separate dataset, so the full claim is not decided by this plan alone.

dataset.name: Database of Clusters of Orthologous Genes (COGs)
dataset.why_it_fits: Provides COG2024 orthologous groups across 2,103 bacterial and 193 archaeal genomes, with downloadable files on the NCBI FTP (COG2024/data). The gene-to-genome membership table and functional category assignments allow computing the fraction of genomes containing each COG and the functional category of universal COGs.
